boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Pultusk entry (battle, 26 December 1806) in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: Marshal Lannes's corps and the 3rd division of Marshal Davout's corps (Gudin's, under General Daultanne) against General Bennigsen's Russian army at Pultusk, from the French approach on 25 December to the Russian retreat in the night and morning of 27 December. Side B's retreat to Pultusk, the orders of 25 and 26 December and the movements of the other French corps are context. The combat of Golymin on the same day, a separate entry, the fighting at Czarnowo and Nasielsk before it, and the pursuit toward Rozan and Ostrolenka after 27 December are outside this entry; the 14 pieces that a Russian column abandoned near Moszyn on the 3rd division's march are reported with their place and time. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) 24 battalions, 27 squadrons and 55 guns, 26,000 men, under Marshal Lannes, and side B (Russian) 66 battalions, 75 squadrons and 200 guns, 44,000 men, under General of Cavalry von Bennigsen, at Pultusk on 26 December 1806. By his stated rule his figures are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. His 66 battalions are Höpfner's 66 for the Russian force at Pultusk, but his 75 squadrons are 20 more than Höpfner's 55 and his 44,000 is 3,400 more than Höpfner's 40,600 (claim hoepfner-side-b; our arithmetic). Höpfner could not determine how many guns were in action and rejects the 150 of Prince Eugen of Württemberg's diary, and Lannes reported about 50 pieces in battery (claims hoepfner-side-b and foucart-side-b), against Bodart's 200 (our comparison). His 24 battalions are Höpfner's 24 for Lannes's corps, without the 9 battalions of Gudin's division that General d'Aultanne brought up, and his 27 squadrons are one more than Höpfner's 26; his 26,000 lies between Höpfner's 'some 20,000' for Lannes's corps and 'about 30,000' with Gudin's division (claim side-a-strength; our comparison). Whether Bodart counts the 3rd division of Davout's corps is not shown. The forces at hand followed both commanders' decisions (claims side-b-command and daultanne-decision), so the phase is unresolved. Which source Bodart used was not checked. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 26/12. Battle at Pultusk (4.)'; 'victory of the French (24 battalions, 27 squadrons, 55 guns = 26,000 men) under Marshal Lannes over the Russians (66 battalions, 75 squadrons, 200 guns = 44,000 men) under General of Cavalry von Bennigsen'. 'Btln.' is Bataillon, 'Esk.' Eskadron, 'Gesch.' Geschütze, 'Gen. d. Kav.' General der Kavallerie and 'M.' Mann in Bodart's list of abbreviations.

claims.value: Side B (Russian) in Höpfner: the Russian forces assembled at Pultusk on 26 December had melted, through the losses suffered, sickness and the detachments of Prince Gallizin and General Pahlen, to 40,600 men: 66 battalions, 55 squadrons, 7 foot and 2½ horse batteries and 5 Cossack pulks. Where the 5 squadrons missing by this count, the Courland dragoons, were on the day could not be determined, nor how many guns were in action; Prince Eugen of Württemberg's diary speaks of 150 guns still present, which Höpfner says cannot be right, and the 3 Prussian batteries with the army in the retreat were not at the battle. The infantry stood in three lines: 21 battalions of the 3rd and 2nd Divisions in the first, 18 in the second and 5 battalions of the 4th and 6th Divisions in the third. General Barclay de Tolly held the projecting wood on the right wing of the main body with the 1st, 3rd and 20th Jäger Regiments, with 2 battalions of the Tenginsk regiment in reserve and its 3rd battalion covering a battery; the Polish horse regiment stood between the wood and Mosino. General Baggowut's reinforced detachment before the left wing had the Starokol and Wilna regiments, 1 battalion of the Reval Musketeer Regiment, the 4th Jäger Regiment, the Tatar Horse Regiment, 2 squadrons of the Kiev Dragoons, 600 Cossacks and a battery, all of the 6th Division. 28 squadrons linked the two, the Cossacks with 10 squadrons of Alexandrov hussars spread out in front, and the cavalry and Cossacks were over 7000 men; a battalion of General Anrepp's 14th Division held the Narew bridge on the left bank while the division marched on to Ostrolenka by the field marshal's order. In the battle Bennigsen sent General Ostermann-Tolstoy with the Tula and 1 more battalion of the Reval regiment in support as far as the ravine; the Tschernigow and Lithuanian musketeer regiments and 20 squadrons went to Barclay; and the Murom and the 2nd battalion of the Reval regiment reinforced Baggowut. 29 Russian battalions did not come into action at all. General Buxhöwden, whom Bennigsen asked to serve as his reserve, returned to Makow with the 5th Division by the field marshal's order.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, the history of side B's ally, read from the page images (pp. 108-111, 113, 114, 116, 118 and 119). He names no source for the 40,600 or the order of battle (dependency note), and his footnotes say what he could not determine. The three lines make 44 battalions (our arithmetic); the passages read do not add the other battalions up to 66. His 40,600 is 3,400 below Bodart's 44,000 and his 55 squadrons 20 below Bodart's 75 (claim bodart-strength; our arithmetic). The force at Pultusk followed Bennigsen's decision to stand and the field marshal's orders to the other divisions (claim side-b-command), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): 'the Russian forces assembled at Pultusk on 26 December had melted, through the losses suffered and sickness, as well as through the detachments of Prince Gallizin and General Pahlen, to 40,600 men'; '66 battalions, 55 squadrons, 7 foot and 2½ horse batteries, 5 Cossack pulks'; 'where the 5 squadrons missing by this count, namely the Courland dragoons, were on the day of the battle could not be determined'; 'how many guns of the army, after deducting those lost and those already sent back, were in action in the battle at Pultusk could not be determined'; 'Prince Eugen of Württemberg says in his diary that 150 guns were still present, which however cannot be right'; 'that heavy artillery had been sent back is confirmed simply by the fact that the 3 Prussian batteries present with the army on the retreat were not present at the battle'; 'the infantry formed in three lines; in the first line 21 battalions of the 3rd and 2nd Divisions; in the second 18, and in the third line 5 battalions of the 4th and 6th Divisions'; 'General Barclay de Tolly held that projecting wood on the right wing of the main body with the 1st, 3rd and 20th Jäger Regiments, against an enemy advancing from Strzegocin as well as from Warsaw'; '2 battalions of the Tenginsk regiment stood in reserve; the 3rd battalion covered a battery that commanded the road to Strzegocin and Golymin; the Polish horse regiment stood between the wood and Mosino'; 'in front of the left wing, or forward of the domain of Gorki, on the road to Warsaw and beyond a ravine that runs down toward the Narew, stood, to cover the Narew bridge and the town as well as the army's left wing, the reinforced detachment of General Baggowut, consisting of the Starokol, the Wilna and 1 battalion of the Reval Musketeer Regiment, the 4th Jäger Regiment, the Tatar Horse Regiment, 2 squadrons of the Kiev Dragoon Regiment, 600 Cossacks and a battery, all troops of the 6th Division'; 'to link this detachment with General Barclay, 28 squadrons, which at first had stood on both' (p. 110); 'wings and in the reserve, had moved forward, and further forward the Cossacks, supported by 10 squadrons of Alexandrov hussars, spread out and swarmed in the bushes in front to observe the enemy' (p. 111); 'the cavalry and Cossacks, over 7000 men strong, stood very suitably to attack and hold up the enemy as he debouched from the woods'; 'a battalion of the 14th Division of General Anrepp held the Narew bridge on the left bank'; 'the division itself, which was on the march to Pultusk, continued its march to Ostrolenka on the left bank in consequence of the field marshal's order'; 'while General Bennigsen, who had the holding of Pultusk particularly at heart, sent General Ostermann-Tolstoy with the Tula and 1 more battalion of the Reval' (p. 113); 'Musketeer Regiment in support as far as the ravine' (p. 114); 'the Tschernigow Musketeer Regiment, standing on the extreme right wing, went forward to support General Barclay, and soon the Lithuanian Musketeer Regiment from what was now the second line and 20 squadrons followed too'; 'General Baggowut was thrown back at all points with the loss of his guns' (p. 117); 'into and over the ravine' (p. 118); 'reinforced by the Murom and the 2nd battalion of the Reval Musketeer Regiment and supported by a battery of General Ostermann, the Russian general went over the ravine again, threw the French back and retook the lost guns'; '29 Russian battalions did not come into action at all'; 'to that end, informing him of his decision, he had at once most urgently asked General Count Buxhöwden to serve him at least as a reserve'; 'in consequence of the field marshal's earlier order, General Count Buxhöwden had already marched off from Makow to Pultusk with the 5th Division very early on the 26th'; 'after a council of war had been held, the general resolved to follow the field marshal's order, and returned to Makow with the troops'.

claims.value: Side B (Russian) in the French reports Foucart prints. Marshal Lannes, on 27 December, put the Russian army that fought him at 40,000 to 50,000 infantry and 5,000 or 6,000 cavalry, with about 50 guns in battery; its advance guard, he wrote, was about 5,000 cavalry and some thousand Cossacks, about 8,000 infantry and 3 cavalry regiments were sent against his right, and his left withstood the fire of about 15,000 men. On 28 December he sent the Emperor the state of the Russian troops at the action and wrote that half of these regiments were in general made up of recruits. General Corbineau wrote on 28 December that it was generally estimated that Lannes had had in front of him 30,000 to 35,000 infantry and 4,500 to 5,000 cavalry, cuirassiers, dragoons, hussars and Cossacks; that the whole left wing of the Russian army appeared to have fought at Pultusk, the corps beaten at Nasielsk among it; and that a fresh corps of 26,000 to 30,000 men under General Buxhœvden at Ostrolenka had taken part neither at Pultusk nor at Golymin. The 3rd corps's journal speaks of the very superior forces of Kamenski's corps.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 462-464, 466, 467 and 514-517). Lannes's 40,000-50,000 infantry and 5,000-6,000 cavalry make 45,000 to 56,000 (our arithmetic), above Höpfner's 40,600 and Bodart's 44,000; Corbineau's figures make 34,500 to 40,000 (our arithmetic), and he gives them as a general estimate, not a count. Lannes's about 50 guns in battery are a quarter of Bodart's 200 (our arithmetic). Lannes was side A's commander reporting the day after the battle; neither he nor Corbineau names a return, and the state of the Russian troops Lannes sent is not printed in the passages read. The phase is unresolved, as in claim hoepfner-side-b. English renderings (ours): Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 27 December 1806'; 'I found the enemy established on the plain before this town; his advance guard' (p. 462); 'was made up of about 5,000 cavalry and some thousand Cossacks' (p. 463); 'at the same time the enemy sent about 8,000 infantry and 3 cavalry regiments against my right, seeking to outflank me'; 'the left withstood the fire of about 15,000 men, and but for a formidable artillery they had at the head of the bridge, whose fire crushed us when we advanced too far, this whole force would have been thrown into the river'; 'I put the Russian army that fought here yesterday at 40,000 to 50,000 infantry and 5,000 or 6,000 cavalry, with about 50 pieces of cannon in battery'; Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 28 December 1806'; 'I have the honour to send Your Majesty the state of the Russian troops that were at the affair of the day before yesterday'; 'half of these regiments in general are made up of recruits'; Corbineau, 'General Corbineau to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 28 December 1806'; 'it is generally estimated that Marshal Lannes' (p. 516); 'had in front of him 30,000 to 35,000 infantry, 4,500 to 5,000 cavalry, cuirassiers, dragoons, hussars and Cossacks' (p. 517); 'it appears that the whole left wing of the Russian army fought at Pultusk and that the corps beaten at Nasielsk was part of it'; 'at Ostrolenka there must be a corps of 26,000 to 30,000 men commanded by General Buxhœvden, with General Kamenski the son and General Essen under his orders; this corps is fresh and took part neither in the combat of Pultusk nor in that of Golymin'; the journal, 'here are the operations of the 3rd division of the 3rd corps during the day of the 26th'; '(extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd corps)'; 'the general, not wishing to commit himself against the very superior forces of Kamenski's corps, was making his dispositions to take up his night position when a heavy cannonade was heard toward Pultusk'.

claims.value: Side A (French). In Höpfner, Marshal Lannes's corps had 24 battalions and 26 squadrons, probably some 20,000 men. It formed in 2 lines: in the first, most of Suchet's division, with General Claparède's advance guard, the 17th light, on the right, covered by Treilhard's light cavalry brigade; the 64th regiment and 1 battalion of the 88th under General Wedell in the centre; and the other battalion of the 88th, the 34th regiment and Becker's dragoon division under Suchet on the left. In the second, 2 regiments of Gazan's division and the 40th regiment of Suchet's, with the 2 battalions of Gazan's 21st regiment in reserve. General d'Aultanne brought up Gudin's division of Davout's corps, 9 battalions, and with it the French forces will have been about 30,000 men. Lannes reported that he placed Suchet's division on two lines and Gazan's behind it, also on two lines. In Foucart's narrative Davout had the retreating Russians followed from 7 in the morning by his 3rd division, General Daultanne, with 170 horses (dragoons and chasseurs); in the 3rd corps's journal 70 chasseurs of the 1st regiment and 100 dragoons of General Rapp led its march, and Daultanne's pencil note says 2 pieces of 8 supported the division. The summary return Foucart prints for the troops that took part in the operations of December 1806 gives the 5th corps 18,400 infantry and 1,100 cavalry and the 3rd corps 21,500 infantry and 750 cavalry present under arms.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (Höpfner pp. 112, 113, 115 and 119; Foucart t. I pp. 462, 463 and 466-469, and t. II the unnumbered page on leaf n486). Höpfner's 'wohl etliche 20,000 Mann' and 'gegen 30,000 Mann' are his estimates and name no source. The return's 5th corps, 18,400 and 1,100, makes 19,500, and its 3rd corps 22,250 (our arithmetic); both rows are whole corps in the middle of December, by Foucart's comment, and the 3rd division's share of the 3rd corps is not given in the passages read, nor which reserve-cavalry row covers Becker's (Beker's) dragoons. Bodart's 24 battalions and 26,000 are compared in claim bodart-strength. Lannes's corps came on Napoleon's order (claim side-a-objectives) and the 3rd division on General Daultanne's own decision (claim daultanne-decision), so the phase is unresolved. Höpfner spells the general d'Aultanne, Foucart's documents Daultanne. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'it consisted of 24 battalions, 26 squadrons, probably some 20,000 men'; 'after defiling from the woods the French deployed parallel to the Russian position in 2 lines; in the first line the greater part of the division Suchet, namely on the right wing the former advance guard under General Claparède, that is the 17th light regiment of that division, covered on the right by the light cavalry brigade Treilhard; in the centre the 64th Regiment and 1 battalion of the 88th Regiment under General Wedell; on the left wing the other battalion of this regiment and the 34th Regiment with the dragoon division Becker, under General Suchet himself'; 'the second line was formed by 2 regiments of the division Gazan and the 40th Regiment of the division Suchet; in reserve followed the 2 battalions of the 21st Regiment of the division Gazan'; 'it was General d'Aultanne with the division Gudin of Davout's corps, 9 battalions'; 'the forces of the French will have amounted to about 30,000 men on the arrival of the division Gudin, so that a definite superiority remained on the Russian side until the last moment'; Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 27 December 1806'; 'I placed the division Suchet on two lines, and that of General Gazan behind it, also on two lines'; Foucart, 'for his part, Marshal Davout, informed that the Russian troops that had spent the night near Strzegocin were retreating on Pultusk by Kensy and Lady, had them followed from 7 in the morning by his 3rd division, General Daultanne, with 170 horses (dragoons and chasseurs)'; the journal, 'here are the operations of the 3rd division of the 3rd corps during the day of the 26th'; '(extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd corps)'; 'day, preceded by 70 chasseurs of the 1st regiment, Captain Hulot, and by 100 dragoons of General Rapp' (p. 467); 'it was probably at this moment that General Daultanne wrote to Marshal Davout the following note in pencil'; 'Marshal Lannes is attacking Pultusk. The 3rd division arrives very opportunely. It falls on the enemy's flank' (p. 468); 'the roads do not allow the artillery to come up; nevertheless 2 8-pounders support the valour of this division' (p. 469); the return, 'summary return of the troops that took part in the operations of the campaign of December 1806'; 'present under arms'; 'infantry | cavalry'; '5th corps | 18,400 | 1,100'; '3rd corps | 21,500 | 750'; 'the summary return above, which is correct since it rests on authentic documents, proves that in the middle of December the whole cavalry of the army did not reach 25,000 horses and that the infantry did not exceed 110,000 men present under arms,'.

claims.value: Bodart names Marshal Lannes as side A's commander and General of Cavalry von Bennigsen as side B's. In Höpfner, Bennigsen resolved to stand at Pultusk in spite of Field Marshal Kaminskoi's definite order for an immediate retreat; Marshal Lannes set his corps in motion again at 7 in the morning of the 26th; and General d'Aultanne brought up Gudin's division of Davout's corps. General Corbineau wrote on 28 December that he had been assured that General Bennigsen lodged at Pultusk on the 26th and commanded the corps that fought Marshal Lannes, with Generals Leewof, Nedmiorasky, Ostermann and Barclay de Tolly and others under his orders.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; Höpfner and Foucart from the page images (Höpfner pp. 108, 112 and 115; Foucart pp. 515 and 516). The commands were set before the battle, so the claim is tagged inherited. Lannes's decision to attack is in claim lannes-decision, Daultanne's to join the battle in claim daultanne-decision and Bennigsen's decisions in claim side-b-command. Lannes's own report has the Russian general in chief commanding in person (claim lannes-on-russian-command). Corbineau's 'On m'a assuré' is hearsay. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'Btln.' is Bataillon, 'Esk.' Eskadron, 'Gesch.' Geschütze, 'Gen. d. Kav.' General der Kavallerie and 'M.' Mann in Bodart's list of abbreviations; Höpfner, 'despite Field Marshal Kaminskoi's definite order for an immediate retreat, General Bennigsen had nevertheless resolved to stand at Pultusk, at the risk of a battle against great superiority and under heavy responsibility'; 'Marshal Lannes had set his corps in motion again at 7 in the morning of the 26th'; 'it was General d'Aultanne with the division Gudin of Davout's corps, 9 battalions'; Corbineau, 'General Corbineau to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 28 December 1806'; 'I have been assured that General Bennigsen lodged at Pultusk on the 26th and that he commanded the corps that fought Marshal Lannes'; 'he had under his orders Generals Leewof, Nedmiorasky, Ostermann and Barclay de Tolly, and some others whom no one could name to me'.

claims.value: Side A's commander decided the attack on the field. In Höpfner, Marshal Lannes set his corps moving again at 7 in the morning of the 26th, reconnoitred in person with 2 squadrons and drove the Cossacks from the woods in front, but could not make out the Russian position because of the height south of Pultusk; he waited for the light infantry and artillery of the advance guard, drove off the Cossack chain with a few cannon shots and had the 17th light occupy the rise. From there, about 10 in the morning, he overlooked the Russian position and soon recognised his opponent's superiority in numbers and the advantages of the defensive in that ground. He had on one side Napoleon's definite order to take the Narew bridge and the certain prospect of no support, the Emperor having told him that he would advance against Golymin with the other corps, and on the other a superior enemy whose presence had evidently not been reckoned on when he was detached; he decided to attack the Russians, and about 11 General Claparède began the attack on General Baggowut's detachment. Lannes reported that he arrived before Pultusk with his corps about 10, and that as soon as he was formed he had the enemy advance guard attacked by the 17th light and the 88th; General Victor was ordered to attack the left bridge with the 34th and a battalion of the 64th, supported by Beker's division, and Lannes sent the rest of the 64th and all the 88th against the right bridge to cut off the enemy's retreat.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (Höpfner pp. 112 and 113; Foucart pp. 462-464). Lannes is side A's commander at this engagement (Bodart), and both accounts show him deciding the attack on the field, so the claim is tagged commander_created; the order to take Pultusk and cross the Narew came from above (claim side-a-objectives). Höpfner's explanation, that the French marshals were too used to the most exact obedience to their Emperor's orders for Lannes to hesitate long, is his own judgement. Lannes's 'pont de gauche' and 'pont de droite' are not reconciled with Höpfner's account of the Russian wings (claim pultusk-ground). English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'Marshal Lannes had set his corps in motion again at 7 in the morning of the 26th'; 'the marshal went forward in person with 2 squadrons to reconnoitre, drove the roving Cossacks out of the woods in front, but could not discover the Russians' position because of the height south of Pultusk'; 'he therefore awaited the arrival of the light infantry and artillery of the advance guard, drove off the advanced chain of Cossacks with a few cannon shots and had the 17th light regiment occupy the gentle height the Cossacks had held'; 'from this height the marshal overlooked the Russian position about 10 in the morning and very soon recognised his opponent's superiority in numbers, as well as the advantages of the defensive in this ground, which made every movement to attack difficult and did not allow the mass of the artillery to be brought into action together with the troops'; 'on the one side Napoleon's definite order to take the Narew bridge and the certain prospect of receiving no support, as the Emperor had told him that he would advance against Golymin with the other corps of the right wing and the centre'; 'side a superior enemy, on whose presence they had evidently not reckoned when the marshal was detached' (p. 113); 'however, the French marshals were too used to the most exact obedience to their Emperor's orders for Marshal Lannes to have long doubted what was to be done in this case; he decided to attack the Russians'; 'in this formation, with a strengthened right wing, the French advanced parallel to the Russian front, and about 11 o'clock General Claparède began the attack on General Baggowut's detachment'; Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 27 December 1806'; 'Sire, I arrived yesterday before Pultusk with my army corps about 10 o'clock'; 'as soon as I was formed, I had the enemy advance guard attacked by the 17th light and the 88th'; 'General Victor received the order to attack the left bridge with the 34th and a battalion of the 64th supported by the division Beker'; 'then I sent the rest of the 64th and the whole 88th against the right bridge to' (p. 463); 'cut off his retreat to the bridge, and I had him attacked by the 17th after a most lively fusillade' (p. 464).

claims.value: The 3rd division of Davout's corps joined the battle on its own general's decision. In Foucart's narrative Davout had it follow the Russian troops retreating on Pultusk from 7 in the morning. In the 3rd corps's journal its general, about to take up his night position rather than commit himself against the very superior forces of Kamenski's corps, heard a heavy cannonade toward Pultusk and continued his movement to approach the 5th corps and second its attacks; the circumstances were too urgent for him to concert with the marshal, but he had him warned of his arrival and of the attack he was going to make. In Höpfner the general, when the heavy fire became audible, believed he had to support Lannes even without an order, and hurried up. Davout sent the division before noon an order to rejoin him, which reached Daultanne when he was already engaged against the Russian extreme right, and after Daultanne's pencil note that Lannes was attacking Pultusk and that the division was falling on the enemy's flank, a second order that reached him only at 3 in the morning. About 8 in the evening Lannes had Daultanne asked not to withdraw, as the 5th corps was going to renew its attacks; in his report Lannes makes no mention of the 3rd division, which fought on his left all day (the editor). The editor writes that the combat of Golymin was fought in analogous circumstances, by army corps that concurred in a common action without general direction for the whole engagement.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (Foucart pp. 462, 466-469, 471 and 473; Höpfner p. 115). Daultanne is not side A's commander in Bodart, and the passages show the decision as his own, not Lannes's, so it is not attributed to Lannes and the phase is unresolved. The editor's comparison with Golymin implies that Pultusk too had no general direction (our reading). Davout's letter to the major general, dated 26 December, enclosed the pencil note. English renderings (ours): Foucart, 'for his part, Marshal Davout, informed that the Russian troops that had spent the night near Strzegocin were retreating on Pultusk by Kensy and Lady, had them followed from 7 in the morning by his 3rd division, General Daultanne, with 170 horses (dragoons and chasseurs)'; the journal, 'here are the operations of the 3rd division of the 3rd corps during the day of the 26th'; '(extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd corps)'; 'the general, not wishing to commit himself against the very superior forces of Kamenski's corps, was making his dispositions to take up his night position when a heavy cannonade was heard toward Pultusk'; 'the general then continued his movement forward to approach the 5th corps and second it in its attacks'; 'the circumstances were too urgent for General Daultanne to concert with the marshal, but he had him warned of his arrival and of the attack he was going to make'; Höpfner, 'it was General d'Aultanne with the division Gudin of Davout's corps, 9 battalions'; 'when, after some halt on the road from Strzegocin to Pultusk, the heavy fire became audible, the general had believed he must support Marshal Lannes even without an order, and had hurried up'; the editor, 'Marshal Davout sent the 3rd division before noon the order to rejoin him,'; 'at the moment this order reached him, General Daultanne was already engaged against the extreme right of the Russians, which he held in check all day and kept from falling on Marshal Lannes's left flank'; 'on receiving this note, Marshal Davout sent General Daultanne a second order, which reached him only at 3 in the morning and gave rise to the following report'; 'it was probably at this moment that General Daultanne wrote to Marshal Davout the following note in pencil'; 'Marshal Lannes is attacking Pultusk. The 3rd division arrives very opportunely. It falls on the enemy's flank' (p. 468); 'the roads do not allow the artillery to come up; nevertheless 2 8-pounders support the valour of this division' (p. 469); 'in his report Marshal Lannes makes no mention of the 3rd division of the 3rd corps, which fought on his left all day'; 'yet General Daultanne, who because of the urgency of the circumstances had been unable to go to the marshal, had at least warned him of his arrival and of the attack he was going to make'; 'the marshal, besides, had him asked about 8 in the evening not to withdraw, as the 5th corps was going to renew its attacks'; 'the combat of Golymin was fought, as we shall see, in analogous circumstances, against columns in retreat coming from different directions, by army corps that concurred in a common action, but without there having been general direction during the whole duration of the engagement'; Davout, 'Marshal Davout to the major general'; 'Garnowo, 26 December 1806'; 'General Daultanne, learning that Marshal Lannes was attacking Pultusk, informed me of it by the enclosed note'.

claims.value: Side B's commander decided to stand. In Höpfner, despite Field Marshal Kaminskoi's definite order for an immediate retreat, General Bennigsen resolved to stand at Pultusk, at the risk of a battle against great superiority and under heavy responsibility: in his view a continued retreat would dissolve the army, make a union of the forces impossible and deliver all the war material to the French, while holding the enemy at Pultusk would give the formations already separated from it time to reunite higher up the Narew. He at once asked General Count Buxhöwden most urgently to serve at least as his reserve. Buxhöwden, already marching from Makow to Pultusk with the 5th Division under the field marshal's earlier order, received a new order to assemble the 5th and 7th Divisions at Makow, take in Bennigsen and go back together to the Russian frontier; after a council of war he obeyed it and returned to Makow. His letter to Bennigsen, which judged an immediate retreat of all the troops the best course and, in agreement with the field marshal, ordered the artillery park sent back to the Russian frontier, reached Bennigsen too late to have any effect. In the battle Bennigsen, intent on holding Pultusk, sent General Ostermann-Tolstoy with the Tula and 1 more battalion of the Reval regiment in support; when the Cossacks reported a strong enemy column on the Strzegocin road, he took back the whole right wing of the main body's infantry so as not to be outflanked, and he had a great battery set up on the flank of the French who had pushed into the wood. After midnight the order to retreat was given, and the retreat began toward the morning of 27 December.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, read from the page images (pp. 108, 109 and 113-118). Bennigsen is side B's commander in Bodart; Höpfner shows him deciding to stand against his superior's order, so the claim is tagged commander_created. Höpfner names no order or report of Bennigsen's for his reasons (dependency note). Lannes's report has the Russian general in chief commanding in person (claim lannes-on-russian-command). English renderings (ours): 'despite Field Marshal Kaminskoi's definite order for an immediate retreat, General Bennigsen had nevertheless resolved to stand at Pultusk, at the risk of a battle against great superiority and under heavy responsibility'; 'a continued retreat must, in the general's view, after the preceding exertions necessarily dissolve the army, make a union of the forces impossible, and in the end deliver all the war material into the hands of the French'; 'all this seemed to the general to amount to a defeat, whereas, if it succeeded in holding up the enemy at Pultusk, the other formations, already separated from Pultusk, gained the time to reunite higher up the Narew'; 'to that end, informing him of his decision, he had at once most urgently asked General Count Buxhöwden to serve him at least as a reserve'; 'in consequence of the field marshal's earlier order, General Count Buxhöwden had already marched off from Makow to Pultusk with the 5th Division very early on the 26th'; 'when, scarcely ½ Meile from Makow, a hussar orderly brought him a letter from the field marshal, in which he found the order to assemble the 5th and 7th Divisions at Makow, to take in General Bennigsen, and to go back together to the Russian frontier'; 'after a council of war had been held, the general resolved to follow the field marshal's order, and returned to Makow with the troops'; 'to General Bennigsen he wrote that an immediate retreat of all the troops to gain time seemed to him the best thing to do, and that in agreement with' (p. 108); 'the field marshal he ordered the artillery park to be sent back at once to the Russian frontier' (p. 109); 'this letter reached General Bennigsen so late that it had to remain wholly without effect'; 'while General Bennigsen, who had the holding of Pultusk particularly at heart, sent General Ostermann-Tolstoy with the Tula and 1 more battalion of the Reval' (p. 113); 'Musketeer Regiment in support as far as the ravine' (p. 114); 'the fight had in this way lasted several hours undecided against the two advanced Russian detachments, when the approach of a strong enemy column on the road from Strzegocin was reported to General Bennigsen by the Cossacks'; 'General Bennigsen could not make out the strength of the new enemy and had to fear being attacked in the right flank by great superiority'; 'he therefore took back the whole right wing of the main body's infantry, so as not to be outflanked'; 'General Bennigsen had a great battery [set up] on the right flank of the [French who had pushed forward] in the wood as far as the road from Strzegocin' (p. 116); '[the French who had] pushed forward [...] set up, and inflicted great losses on them' (p. 117); 'the Russians rested in the position they had held until after midnight, when the order to retreat was given, which was indeed fully justified by the circumstances and was begun toward the morning of 27 December'.

claims.value: Bodart codes the battle of Pultusk on 26 December 1806 as a victory of the French under Marshal Lannes over the Russians under General of Cavalry von Bennigsen. Lannes reported on 27 December that the force of about 8,000 infantry and 3 cavalry regiments the enemy had sent against his right, attacked by the 17th light, had been overthrown and had come back to the bridge in the greatest disorder; that the enemy, seeing his left forced about 3 in the afternoon, had detached a column from his right to try a second time to outflank the French right; that the fighting lasted from 10 in the morning until 6 in the evening; and that the enemy, harassed all night, had been able to pass only part of his troops to the left bank, the rest filing off by the right bank of the Narew on Rozan; the bridge had been burnt. The 3rd corps's journal records that the night of the 26th to the 27th was extremely quiet, and that General Daultanne, learning that the enemy had recrossed the Narew and that Lannes met no difficulty in entering Pultusk, set off at 8 in the morning to rejoin the 3rd corps. General Corbineau wrote on 28 December that the corps that had fought Lannes had withdrawn on Rozan by the right bank of the Narew and that Lannes was master of the Narew. In Höpfner the Russians rested in their position until after midnight, when the order to retreat was given, and the retreat began toward the morning of 27 December.
claims.rationale: Bodart's heading and entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; Foucart and Höpfner from the page images (pp. 462, 464, 466, 471, 473 and 515; Höpfner p. 118). The sources read agree that side B left Pultusk to side A in the night and morning after the battle; they differ on how the fighting ended (claims hoepfner-result and side-a-reports-on-the-evening). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 27 December 1806'; 'at the same time the enemy sent about 8,000 infantry and 3 cavalry regiments against my right, seeking to outflank me'; 'then I sent the rest of the 64th and the whole 88th against the right bridge to' (p. 463); 'cut off his retreat to the bridge, and I had him attacked by the 17th after a most lively fusillade' (p. 464); 'the enemy was overthrown and came back to the bridge in the greatest disorder'; 'the enemy, seeing his left forced about 3 in the afternoon, detached a column from his right to try a second time to outflank our right, but the presence of General Gazan was enough to make it go back into line'; 'we fought from 10 in the morning until 6 in the evening in mud up to mid-thigh'; 'the enemy, having been harassed all night, could pass only part of his troops to the left bank. The other part is filing off by the right bank of the Narew on Rozan'; 'the bridge was burnt; it is being repaired'; the journal, 'here are the operations of the 3rd division of the 3rd corps during the day of the 26th'; '(extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd corps)'; 'the night of the 26th to the 27th was extremely quiet'; 'General Daultanne, having learned that the enemy had recrossed the Narew and that Marshal Lannes met no difficulty in entering Pultusk, set off at 8 in the morning to rejoin the 3rd corps at Garnowo'; '(journal of operations of the 3rd corps)'; Corbineau, 'General Corbineau to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 28 December 1806'; 'the corps that fought against Marshal Lannes at Pultusk withdrew on Rozan by the right bank of the Narew,'; 'Marshal Lannes is master of the Narew'; Höpfner, 'the Russians rested in the position they had held until after midnight, when the order to retreat was given, which was indeed fully justified by the circumstances and was begun toward the morning of 27 December'.

claims.value: Höpfner gives a different result. Both sides, he writes, claim the victory, and the victory of the Russians is hardly to be doubted: Lannes was repulsed at all points, and Bennigsen's retreat the next day, after the attack had been beaten off, lay in circumstances that the marshal had no part in shaping. In his account more about the night fight in the wood could hardly be stated or cleared up now, but the result on the French left is certain: the French were thrown back there with loss. On the French right, General Baggowut, after being thrown back over the ravine with the loss of his guns, recrossed it with reinforcements, threw the French back and retook the lost guns, and General Somow decided the fight there for the Russians with a bayonet attack of the Tula regiment after dark. Lannes led his troops back into the position they had held before the attack, and General d'Aultanne posted himself at the edge of the woods behind, on the Strzegocin road, to secure the marshal's left flank. By Russian statements in his footnote the French withdrew further, and General Lambert, left behind when the Russian army marched off the next morning, found nothing of the French on the field and far beyond but wounded and much baggage and guns that could not be moved. The Russians lost no guns in the battle itself.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, read from the page images (pp. 117-119). A different result from Bodart's frozen victory of the French (claim bodart-winner), kept as a dispute and not resolved. Höpfner sets the Russian against the French reports on the fight in the wood (claim side-a-reports-on-the-evening) before giving his result; side A's own documents on the evening are in claim side-a-reports-on-the-evening. English renderings (ours): 'both sides ascribe the victory to themselves'; 'the victory of the Russians is hardly to be doubted; Marshal Lannes was repulsed at all points, and if General Bennigsen had the retreat begun the next day after the attack had been beaten off, this lay in circumstances in whose shaping the marshal had no part'; 'to state and clear up anything more about this night fight would hardly be practicable now'; 'the result is certain, that the French were thrown back with loss on their left wing'; 'General Baggowut was thrown back at all points with the loss of his guns' (p. 117); 'into and over the ravine' (p. 118); 'reinforced by the Murom and the 2nd battalion of the Reval Musketeer Regiment and supported by a battery of General Ostermann, the Russian general went over the ravine again, threw the French back and retook the lost guns'; 'until General Somow with the Tula Musketeer Regiment, by a bayonet attack, decided the fight on this wing too in favour of the Russians, after darkness had already fallen'; 'Marshal Lannes led his troops back into the position they had held before the attack'; 'General d'Aultanne posted himself at the edge of the woods lying behind, on the road to Strzegocin, to secure the marshal's left flank'; 'by Russian statements the French had withdrawn further, and General Lambert, who had been left behind the next morning when the Russian army marched off, had found nothing of the French on the battlefield and far beyond it but wounded rolling about in the mud and a mass of baggage and guns that no human power could have carried away'; 'the Russians lost no guns in the battle itself'.

claims.value: Side A's own documents on how the fighting ended. General Daultanne reported to Marshal Davout, under the date 26 December 1806, that very unfortunate events had occurred: despite the 3rd division's efforts to second the attack of Lannes's troops on Pultusk, it had not been possible to become decidedly master of the position, which had been taken, but Lannes's troops could not hold it; the division had to keep its ground until 8 in the evening, had to yield to circumstances and was very lucky to have been able to make a retrograde movement. In the 3rd corps's journal the 34th regiment (5th corps), facing very superior forces in the darkness, was forced to retreat; after the most vigorous cavalry charge, about 8 in the evening, an hour passed without a shot, the 5th corps was found occupying the same position as before the action, and Daultanne took position at the edge of the wood a few hundred paces off. Lannes wrote that if a battalion of the 88th, charged by cavalry, had not given way, the whole enemy column would have been taken. In Höpfner the French reports say that darkness fell over the infantry fight in the wood and d'Aultanne lost touch with Lannes in it; that the Russians threw themselves with cavalry into the gap and on the right flank of Gudin's division; that several battalions of the division were broken and General Suchet's battalions thrown back in disorder toward the woods, and only the 85th, in the second line of Gudin's division, received the Russians calmly and threw them back; and that the last attack took place at 8 in the evening, when a violent storm ended all fighting.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (Foucart pp. 462, 464, 466, 469-472; Höpfner p. 117). These are side A's documents and French reports; they report the position taken and not held and the 5th corps back where it started, but do not call the result a defeat, and Lannes's report of the 27th claims the enemy overthrown (claim bodart-winner). They agree with Höpfner's account that Lannes's troops returned to their starting position (claim hoepfner-result; our comparison). Daultanne's report, dated 26 December, answered an order that reached him at 3 in the morning (claim daultanne-decision). English renderings (ours): Daultanne, 'General Daultanne to Marshal Davout at Skaszewo or Golymin'; 'Przewodowo, 26 December 1806'; 'I have the honour to report to you that since my last report very unfortunate events have occurred, since, despite the unhappy efforts the 3rd division was able to make to second the attack of Marshal Lannes's troops on Pultusk, it was not possible to become decidedly master of this position, which had nevertheless been taken,' (p. 471); 'but the troops of Marshal Lannes could not hold it' (p. 472); 'the 3rd division was obliged to keep its ground until 8 in the evening'; 'it was necessary to yield to the circumstances, and [we were] very lucky to have been able to make a retrograde movement in the difficult position in which events had placed these troops'; the journal, 'here are the operations of the 3rd division of the 3rd corps during the day of the 26th'; '(extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd corps)'; 'meanwhile the 34th regiment (5th corps), having had to deal with very superior forces, and the darkness of the night not allowing it to judge the enemy's movements well, was forced to retreat'; 'the lines still had to withstand several cavalry charges, the most vigorous of which took place about 8 in the evening, at the moment when a terrible storm was heard and, driven by a violent wind, the snow was falling in large flakes'; 'an hour having passed without a single musket shot being heard, the 5th corps was reconnoitred and found occupying the same position as before the action,'; 'which decided General Daultanne to take position at the edge of the wood a few hundred paces off and to have the division, which was exhausted with fatigue, bivouac there,'; Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 27 December 1806'; 'if a battalion of the 88th, which was charged by the cavalry, had not given way, this whole column would have been prisoners of war'; Höpfner, 'the French reports state, on the contrary, that darkness fell over the infantry fight in the wood, that General d'Aultanne lost touch with Marshal Lannes in it, and that the Russians, with the cavalry brought up, threw themselves into the gap and on the right flank of the division Gudin'; 'thereupon several battalions of the division were broken, and General Suchet's battalions thrown back in disorder toward the woods,'; 'and only the 85th Regiment in the second line of the division Gudin received the Russians calmly and threw them back'; 'and the last attack took place at 8 in the evening, when a violent storm put an end to all fighting'.

claims.rationale: Bodart's printed losses, read from the page image in the frame transcription. His 700 French prisoners are Höpfner's 700 prisoners actually taken by the Russians, and his Russian 3,500 the 3500 dead and wounded of the Russian reports in Höpfner (claims side-a-losses-reported and side-b-losses-reported; our comparison). His 12 cannon are the 12 guns the French said they found on the field, while Höpfner says the Russians lost no guns in the battle itself. His French 3,300 killed and wounded lie above the 6—700 dead and 1500 wounded the French gave, 2,100 to 2,200 (our arithmetic), and Lannes's figures, and below the Russians' 7000. claims.value: Side A's losses as reported. Lannes put the loss of his corps, killed and wounded, at about 1,000 men on 27 December: General Boussart and General Treillard were wounded and their horses killed, General Claparède's horse was killed and General Vedel was wounded twice; the dragoon division had 22 men killed, 2 of them officers, and 34 dragoons wounded, 2 of them officers, with 88 horses killed and 22 wounded. On 28 December he wrote that, from what he had seen, his dead and wounded were more numerous than he had reported the day before. General Corbineau wrote that the marshal estimated his loss at 700 wounded and 400 killed. A line in Foucart's small type gives the 3rd division 2 officers and 85 men killed and 19 officers and 516 men wounded, and Daultanne reported many wounded, especially in the 12th and 21st regiments. In Höpfner the French give their loss as 6—700 dead and 1500 wounded, among them Generals Claparède, Wedell and Bonnard, Lannes being slightly wounded; the Russians believe they put about 7000 French out of action, by the official reports even 10,000; 700 prisoners were actually taken; the French admit in their report only that one battalion of the 88th was surprised by the Russian cavalry and largely destroyed; and Höpfner, who calls the losses impossible to state, holds that the French loss must have been considerably greater than the Russian.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (Foucart pp. 462, 465, 471, 472 and 514-516; Höpfner pp. 114, 118 and 119). Lannes's about 1,000 is for his corps only, and he revised it upward the next day; Corbineau's 700 wounded and 400 killed make 1,100 (our arithmetic), the marshal's estimate at second hand. The 3rd division's line, which names no source, makes 87 killed and 535 wounded, 622 in all (our arithmetic), for the division Lannes's report omits (claim daultanne-decision). The French figures in Höpfner make 2,100 to 2,200 (our arithmetic), and he does not name the French report; his view that the loss was greater is his inference from the artillery fire and the failed attacks. Bodart's 700 prisoners and 3,300 are compared in claim bodart-losses. claims.value: Side B's losses as reported. In Höpfner the Russian reports put their own loss at 3500 dead and wounded, while the French state that after the Russians' retreat they found on the field over 2000 dead, 1500 wounded who could not be moved, 12 guns and many vehicles of all kinds; Höpfner says the Russians lost no guns in the battle itself and that the loss of both sides cannot be stated. Lannes reported on 27 December that the enemy had left on the field over 3,000 killed and wounded, some pieces of cannon and many caissons, that 1,000 to 1,200 wounded were found in the town and that about 600 prisoners were taken; on 28 December, that many more Russian dead had been found on the field than had been thought, the 34th alone having killed 800 to 1,000, and that the houses and churches of the town were full of wounded. Corbineau wrote that the town was full of Russian wounded and stragglers, estimated at 2,000, and that 600 prisoners able to bear arms, many officers among them, were taken in the battle. On the 3rd division's march its scouts reported a body of cavalry covering a Russian column of artillery and baggage stuck in the mud between Kensy and Lady; when the division's first echelon advanced to charge, the cavalry was driven back behind the village of Moszyn, abandoning 14 pieces of ordnance and many wagons (the journal), and Davout wrote that the enemy fell back at the approach of the troops and abandoned 14 pieces, many caissons and baggage. Daultanne wrote that the movement Davout ordered forced him to abandon 23 pieces of cannon that the enemy had had to leave.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (Höpfner pp. 118 and 119; Foucart pp. 462, 465-467, 471-473 and 514-516). Höpfner's Russian 3500 is Bodart's 3,500 (claim bodart-losses); the French count of over 2000 dead and 1500 wounded makes over 3,500 (our arithmetic), near Lannes's over 3,000 left on the field. Lannes's 1,000-1,200 and Corbineau's 2,000 wounded and stragglers in the town may overlap the wounded left on the field (our reading). The 14 pieces were abandoned on the 3rd division's march, before it reached the field (the journal); whether the 23 pieces include them, and whether any are Bodart's 12 cannon, is not shown. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'to state the loss of both sides in the battle is quite impossible'; 'the Russian reports put their own loss at 3500 dead and wounded'; 'the French on the other hand state that after the Russians' retreat they [had] found over 2000 dead, 1500 wounded who could not be transported, 12 guns and many vehicles of all kinds on the battlefield' (p. 118); '[had] found' (p. 119); 'the Russians lost no guns in the battle itself'; Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 27 December 1806'; 'the enemy left on the battlefield, killed as well as wounded, more than 3,000 men, some pieces of cannon and many caissons'; 'we found 1,000 to 1,200 wounded in the town'; 'we took about 600 prisoners'; Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 28 December 1806'; 'I had the battlefield gone over this morning, and many more Russian dead were found than had been thought'; 'the 34th alone killed 800 to 1,000 of them'; 'there are also many more wounded in the town than was expected; the houses and the churches are full'; Corbineau, 'General Corbineau to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 28 December 1806'; 'the town is full of Russian wounded and stragglers; their number is estimated at 2,000'; 'during the battle 600 prisoners were taken in' (p. 515); 'a state to bear arms, among whom there are a great number of officers' (p. 516); the journal, 'here are the operations of the 3rd division of the 3rd corps during the day of the 26th'; '(extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd corps)'; 'the 3rd division had scarcely come out of the village of Strzegocin when it was warned by its scouts that a fairly considerable body of cavalry was covering the march of a column of artillery and baggage that was stuck in the mud between Kensy and Lady'; claims.value: Pultusk is a town in Russian Poland on the right bank of the Narew, 50 km north of Warsaw (Bodart). In Höpfner the battlefield is bounded on the east by the Narew and on the south and south-west by woods, rises gently northward from them and falls again toward Pultusk, so that a gently rising but fairly extended height hides a position at Pultusk from an enemy coming out of the woods; in the thaw the rich loam had dissolved into a pulp that hindered every arm, and guns could be moved only with the utmost exertion; the approach through the woods bounding the field on the west seems to have been particularly difficult. The Russian left leaned on Pultusk and the right on the wood of Mosino; General Baggowut stood on the road to Warsaw beyond a ravine running down to the Narew; the Mosino brook, in that season, did not allow a wider turning movement, so the wood had to be taken; and woods a few thousand paces off in front hid the enemy's strength. Lannes found the enemy established on the plain before the town, his right resting on a bridge at the far end of the town and his left on another bridge at its entrance; his men fought in mud to mid-thigh, the wind and hail knocked them over, and all his artillery stuck in the marshes. In the 3rd corps's journal the thaw had been complete for two days, rare in Poland in that season; the ground was clayey and marshy and the roads frightful, two hours being needed for a short league; the enemy was formed on the plateau of Pultusk, his right, bent back at a right angle, crowning the heights over Moszyn; and that part of his line would have been thrown into the ravine of Bialowizna but for a strong reserve posted in a thicket parallel to the road. The journal of the 5th dragoon division, quoted by the editor, has marshy ground where the horses sank in the mud to their bellies and shifting, very muddy ground before the town. On 28 December Lannes wrote that one could not take a step without sinking into the mud to mid-thigh; the editor's note and Corbineau give the Narew as 25 to 30 toises wide at Pultusk.
claims.rationale: Bodart's location line, read from the page image in the frame transcription; Höpfner and Foucart from the page images (Höpfner pp. 109-112; Foucart pp. 462-464, 466-469, 514, 515 and 517). The ground and the weather were given, so the claim is tagged inherited; the choice of the position was Bennigsen's (claim side-b-command). Lannes's two bridges are not reconciled with Höpfner's wings, which rest on the town and the Mosino wood (our comparison). The dragoon journal's first paragraph is dated 'Le 22' as printed, though its note mark is set in Lannes's account of the 26th; the figure is not corrected. Höpfner's plan of the battle was not inspected. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '1806 26/12. Battle at Pultusk (4.)'; 'victory of the French (24 battalions, 27 squadrons, 55 guns = 26,000 men) under Marshal Lannes over the Russians (66 battalions, 75 squadrons, 200 guns = 44,000 men) under General of Cavalry von Bennigsen'; '(town in Russian Poland, on the right bank of the Narew, 50 km north of Warsaw)'; Höpfner, 'the battlefield at Pultusk is bounded on the east by the Narew, on the south and south-west by woods, rises gently from these woods toward the north and falls again toward Pultusk, so that from an enemy debouching from these woods a position at Pultusk is hidden by a gently rising but fairly extended height'; 'but at the time of the battle, the thaw having set in, the rich loam soil had dissolved into a pulp, so that every arm found an obstacle in it, and the movement of the guns could be accomplished only with the utmost exertion'; 'an approach to the Russian position through the woods that bound the battlefield on the west seems to have been particularly difficult'; 'the left wing leaned on Pultusk, the right wing on the wood of Mosino'; 'on the road to Warsaw and beyond a ravine that runs down toward the Narew'; 'as the state of the Mosino brook in that season did not well allow a wider turning movement, so that the enemy necessarily had to take that wood to advance further'; 'the flaw of the position at Pultusk, that it was surrounded in front, at a few thousand paces' distance, by wood that hid the enemy's strength and dispositions'; Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 27 December 1806'; 'I found the enemy established on the plain before this town; his advance guard' (p. 462); 'the enemy fell back on his main body, which had its right resting on the bridge at the far end of the town, and its left on another bridge at the entrance of the town'; 'we fought from 10 in the morning until 6 in the evening in mud up to mid-thigh'; 'Your Majesty saw the weather of the day; the wind and the hail knocked our soldiers over'; 'all our artillery had stuck in the marshes, and despite all General Foucher's efforts it could hardly serve us and it is at this moment in bad condition...'; 'the ground the army was crossing was clayey and marshy; the roads were frightful... Two hours were needed to cover a short league'; 'the enemy was formed on the plateau of Pultusk, on which he rested his left, and his right, bending back at a right angle, crowned the heights that overhang Moszyn'; 'this part of the enemy line would have been entirely thrown into the ravine of Bialowizna but for the help of a strong reserve which, placed in a thicket parallel to the road, stopped our first echelons'; the dragoon journal, 'on the 22nd, as soon as the 5th corps could defile at 10 in the morning, the division moved into the position it had occupied the day before'; 'the 1st brigade, General Boussart, directed to the left, followed the movements of the division Suchet in marshy ground where the horses sank in the mud up to their bellies, and so intimidated the enemy that he did not dare to undertake a charge'; 'the 2nd brigade, General Viallannes, stayed alone facing the town, occupying the centre of the army corps on shifting and very muddy ground, manoeuvring under the enemy's guns and opposing every attempt at this point'; '(journal of march of the 5th dragoon division)'; Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 28 December 1806'; 'it is impossible to form an idea of the country; one cannot take a step without sinking into the mud up to mid-thigh'; the editor, 'the Narew is 25 to 30 toises wide at Pultusk'; Corbineau, 'General Corbineau to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 28 December 1806'; 'the width of the river is 25 to 30 toises'.

claims.value: Side A's means. In Höpfner, the march on Pultusk, continued with Becker's dragoon division, brought the main body of the advance guard, the cavalry and Suchet's division in the evening only to Zbroszki, and Gazan's division to Vinica, so that the troops covered only 2¾ Meilen in about 14 hours, and part of the artillery was brought along only with the most incredible efforts. At Pultusk the artillery that had come along stood on the right wing and in the centre, while the left wing had been unable to bring any guns. Lannes reported that all his artillery stuck in the marshes and, despite all General Foucher's efforts, could hardly serve and was now in bad condition; that the country offered no resources, having been totally ravaged by the Russians; and that a bridge at Sierock would serve to draw supplies from Warsaw. On 28 December he wrote that all the artillery had at last been got out of the mud; Corbineau wrote that it had, except for some caissons and two pieces, and that Pultusk would offer no resources to the corps occupying it, the country for several leagues around being marshy and sterile. The 3rd division doubled the teams of an 8-pounder to bring it near Moszyn; Daultanne's pencil note says the roads did not let the artillery come up, though 2 pieces of 8 supported the division, and his report says the munitions were exhausted and it was almost impossible to bring up the caissons.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (Höpfner pp. 107 and 113; Foucart pp. 462, 464, 466, 468, 469, 471, 472 and 514-516). The sentence on the march begins on Höpfner's p. 106, which is not registered, so its subject and date are not cited here. The ground and the thaw were given, while the march and the order of battle were commanders' choices, so the phase is unresolved. claims.value: Side B's means. In Höpfner the Russians at Pultusk lacked everything: no preparations at all had been made to supply the army regularly in that inhospitable region, everything having been reckoned only for a march through; the contractor then given the supply made many promises that he could not keep for lack of ready money, so that the troops struggled continually with the greatest want. Ammunition was as short, and on the 25th General Löwenstern had to go back to Tykoczyn to bring up ammunition from the reserve park. The French cavalry's reconnaissance before Pultusk on the afternoon of the 25th alarmed the Russian troops, already overstrained, who believed they could not rest fully and camped in order of battle that night. Heavy artillery had been sent back, and the 3 Prussian batteries with the army in the retreat were not at the battle. General Corbineau wrote that a Russian magazine of grain and flour at Pultusk had been shipped to Ostrolenka by the Narew, and that the Russians' main hospital and administrations were at Ostrolenka on the 26th.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (Höpfner pp. 107 and 109; Foucart pp. 515 and 517). Höpfner names no source for the supply (dependency note). The want was inherited from the retreat, while the decision to stand at Pultusk was Bennigsen's (claim side-b-command), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'the Russians at Pultusk lacked everything'; 'no preparations at all had been made to supply the army regularly in these inhospitable regions, since everything had been reckoned only for the march through'; 'in the emergency the supply was now given to a Jewish contractor, who, so as not to miss the lucrative business, made many promises that he could not keep for lack of ready money, so that the troops had to struggle continually with the greatest want'; 'ammunition was lacking just as much, although they had as yet come little to grips with the enemy, and as early as the 25th General Löwenstern had to go back to Tykoczyn to bring up ammunition from the reserve park'; 'the heads of the French cavalry arrived before Pultusk to reconnoitre as early as the afternoon of the 25th, when the first Russian troops had scarcely arrived there from Strzegocin'; 'yet this alarm had the great disadvantage that the Russian troops, who had already suffered such excessive exertions, believed they could not give themselves up to complete rest, but camped in order of battle already in the night'; 'that heavy artillery had been sent back is confirmed simply by the fact that the 3 Prussian batteries present with the army on the retreat were not present at the battle'; Corbineau, 'General Corbineau to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 28 December 1806'; 'a magazine of grain and flour that the Russians had at Pultusk was loaded on boats and carried to Ostrolenka by the Narew'; 'the Russians' main hospital and their administrations were at Ostrolenka on the 26th'.

claims.value: Side A's information. The major general's letter of 25 December told Lannes what was presumed: the division beaten on the Wkra had withdrawn to Strzegocin and was thought to be going on to Pultusk or Golymin, and one or two regiments might still be at Sierock. In Foucart's narrative Lannes knew of the enemy's march on Pultusk from General Beker's reconnaissance of the 25th, and in Höpfner the heads of the French cavalry reconnoitred before Pultusk that afternoon. The end of a headquarters letter, printed by Foucart just before his narrative of the morning of the battle, says that it was not yet known whether Lannes had taken Pultusk. In Höpfner, Lannes's own reconnaissance could not discover the Russian position because of the height south of Pultusk, and only about 10, from the rise, did he see it and recognise his opponent's superiority in numbers; the Emperor had told him that he would advance against Golymin with the other corps, so he could expect no support. General d'Aultanne had Lannes informed of his approach and reconnoitred the Russian position in person; in the 3rd corps's journal the circumstances were too urgent for him to concert with the marshal; the division's scouts had reported the cavalry covering a Russian column; an 8-pounder fired on the village of Moszyn to make the enemy unmask his forces, but only a few hundred Cossacks came out; and in the dark the 34th could not judge the enemy's movements. Davout's second order reached Daultanne only at 3 in the morning, and Lannes's report of 27 December makes no mention of the 3rd division (the editor).

claims.value: Side B's information, in Höpfner. The French cavalry's reconnaissance before Pultusk on the afternoon of the 25th alarmed the Russians, who camped that night in order of battle. The flaw of the position was that woods a few thousand paces off in front hid the enemy's strength and dispositions, though the great vigilance of the Cossacks, present wherever the enemy could be expected, partly made up for it. On the morning of 26 December the Cossacks reported the enemy's approach from several sides; the French left wing was hidden by wooded ground, so the Russians could not see the French strength there. After several hours of fighting the Cossacks reported a strong enemy column on the Strzegocin road; Bennigsen could not make out the strength of this new enemy and had to fear an attack on his right flank by great superiority, so he took back his right wing. Buxhöwden's letter, which judged an immediate retreat of all the troops the best course, reached Bennigsen too late to have any effect. Höpfner explains the Russians' purely defensive conduct in part by their poor view of the enemy's strength in the bushy terrain, especially on the right wing.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, read from the page images (pp. 107-109, 112, 113, 115, 116 and 119); he names no source for the Russian reports he summarises (dependency note). claims.value: Side A's objectives. The major general wrote to Lannes on 25 December that the Emperor intended him to leave Nasielsk for Pultusk, cross the Narew there and build a bridgehead at once, with Beker's division under his orders besides his light cavalry; in Höpfner Lannes had Napoleon's definite order to take the Narew bridge. The end of a headquarters letter, printed by Foucart just before his narrative of the morning of the battle, has Davout's corps stay at Golymin with one of its divisions on the high road to Pultusk, to act if necessary, as it was not yet known whether Lannes had taken Pultusk. Davout had his 3rd division follow the Russians retreating on Pultusk; its general continued his movement to approach the 5th corps and second its attacks, and Davout's order sent before noon called it back to him.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (Foucart pp. 439, 440, 462, 466, 467 and 471; Höpfner p. 112). Lannes's objective was set from above, while the 3rd division's was its own general's decision (claim daultanne-decision), so the claim's single phase is unresolved. On the headquarters letter, see claim side-a-information. claims.value: Side B's objective in Höpfner: by the halt at Pultusk General Bennigsen wanted nothing but a pause in the retreat and to hold up the enemy; even at best he could not think of taking the offensive again; the Russians did not seek the tactical decision but accepted it only where it could not be avoided; and holding the enemy at Pultusk would give the formations already separated from it time to reunite higher up the Narew. The position covered the Russian line of retreat on Ostrolenka, and in the worst case the Narew bridge had to be held for a retreat to the left bank and the link with Anrepp's division. The Russians wanted nothing else than to beat off an attack, which they fully achieved with great economy of force.
claims.rationale: Höpfner, read from the page images (pp. 108, 109, 111 and 119). Bennigsen chose to stand against his superior's order (claim side-b-command), so the claim is tagged commander_created. Höpfner gives the aim as his own reading of Bennigsen's conduct; he names no order or report of Bennigsen's. claims.value: Side A attacked. Bodart has a victory of the French. In Höpfner, Lannes decided to attack the Russians; the French advanced parallel to the Russian front, and about 11 General Claparède began the attack on General Baggowut's detachment, while General Suchet attacked the Mosino wood with the 34th regiment; later General d'Aultanne attacked the Russian right flank with half battalions at 50 paces' interval, and the French right and centre went to the attack again. Lannes reported that as soon as he was formed he had the enemy's advance guard attacked, then ordered the left bridge attacked and sent troops against the right bridge; the 3rd corps's journal has the 3rd division attack the enemy's flank by half battalions and echelons at 50 paces. Side B defended its position. Its charges and counterattacks were made within it: General Koschin's attack on Wedell's flank, Barclay's renewed attack, Baggowut's recrossing of the ravine and Somow's bayonet attack (Höpfner); and Lannes reported that the enemy sent about 8,000 infantry and 3 cavalry regiments against his right to outflank him, and later a column from his right to try again. In Höpfner the Russians only beat off the French attacks and nowhere made a counterstroke, and 29 Russian battalions never came into action.
claims.rationale: Coded A_attacked: side A attacked side B's position at Pultusk; side B's charges and counterattacks were made within its own defended position, which by the brief do not make the defender an attacker, and Höpfner says the Russians nowhere made a counterstroke. Lannes, side A's commander at this engagement (Bodart), decided the attack on the field (claim lannes-decision), so the claim is tagged commander_created; the order to take Pultusk came from above (claim side-a-objectives), and the 3rd division's attack was its own general's decision (claim daultanne-decision). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Höpfner, 'however, the French marshals were too used to the most exact obedience to their Emperor's orders for Marshal Lannes to have long doubted what was to be done in this case; claims.value: The passages read name no works on either side in the fighting. Side B held the town, the Mosino wood and the ground beyond a ravine, with the main body's artillery in front of the first line at the most favourable points and a battery commanding the road to Strzegocin and Golymin (Höpfner); Lannes wrote that a formidable artillery the enemy had at the head of the bridge crushed his men whenever they advanced too far; and the 3rd corps's journal has a strong Russian reserve posted in a thicket parallel to the road. In Höpfner Bennigsen had a great battery set up on the flank of the French in the wood during the battle. Side A was ordered on 25 December to build a bridgehead once across the Narew; on 28 December, after the Russians had gone, Lannes held the left bank at the bridgehead with a company of grenadiers (Corbineau).
claims.rationale: Coded none_named: the cited passages describe where both sides stood and name no entrenchments, redoubts, abatis or other works used in the fighting. Lannes's 'à la tête du pont' places artillery at the end of the bridge without naming a work (our reading), and a battery or a thicket is not a work under the brief. The bridgehead of the order of 25 December was to be built after the crossing, and the one Corbineau names on the 28th was held after the battle. none_named reports the passages read, not proof that no works existed; Höpfner's plan of the battle was not inspected. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'the left wing leaned on Pultusk, the right wing on the wood of Mosino'; 'the artillery of the main body stood in front of the first line, placed at the most favourable points'; '2 battalions of the Tenginsk regiment stood in reserve; the 3rd battalion covered a battery that commanded the road to Strzegocin and Golymin; the Polish horse regiment stood between the wood and Mosino'; 'on the road to Warsaw and beyond a ravine that runs down toward the Narew'; 'General Bennigsen had a great battery [set up] on the right flank of the [French who had pushed forward] in the wood as far as the road from Strzegocin' (p. 116); '[the French who had] pushed forward [...] set up, and inflicted great losses on them' (p. 117); Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 27 December 1806'; 'the left withstood the fire of about 15,000 men, and but for a formidable artillery they had at the head of the bridge, whose fire crushed us when we advanced too far, this whole force would have been thrown into the river'; the journal, 'here are the operations of the 3rd division of the 3rd corps during the day of the 26th'; '(extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd corps)'; 'this part of the enemy line would have been entirely thrown into the ravine of Bialowizna but for the help of a strong reserve which, placed in a thicket parallel to the road, stopped our first echelons'; the major general, 'the major general to Marshal Lannes'; 'Slostowo, 25 December 1806'; 'the Emperor's intention, Marshal, is that you leave Nasielsk to make for Pultusk, cross the Narew there and build a bridgehead there at once'; Corbineau, 'General Corbineau to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 28 December 1806'; 'he has on the left bank, at the bridgehead, a company of grenadiers'.

Bodart's 24 battalions and 26,000 match Lannes's corps without the 3rd division of Davout's corps (Höpfner's 24 battalions and 'some 20,000'), while Höpfner puts the French with that division at about 30,000; no passage read gives the 3rd division's strength on 26 December beyond its 9 battalions, 170 horses and 2 guns, and the summary return in t. II gives only whole corps. The pages of 28 December (pp. 514-517) were the one targeted follow-up: they add Lannes's revised view of his losses and Corbineau's figures for the losses, the prisoners and the Russian strength, but not Lannes's position return. A return of the 3rd corps for late December, or the fold-out situations in t. II, could close the gap.

Disputes kept as separate claims or within them: the result (a French victory, Bodart; both sides claimed it and the Russian victory is hardly to be doubted, Höpfner; the position taken but not held, Daultanne's report and the 3rd corps's journal); the Russian command (Bennigsen, Bodart, Höpfner and Corbineau's hearsay; the Russian general in chief in person with Bennigsen, Lannes); side B's strength (44,000, Bodart; 40,600, Höpfner; 40,000 to 50,000 infantry and 5,000 or 6,000 cavalry, Lannes; 30,000 to 35,000 infantry and 4,500 to 5,000 cavalry, Corbineau's general estimate); side B's squadrons and guns (75 squadrons and 200 guns, Bodart; 55 squadrons and 7 foot and 2½ horse batteries, with the guns in action undetermined and Prince Eugen's 150 rejected, Höpfner; about 50 pieces in battery, Lannes); side A's strength (26,000, Bodart; some 20,000 for Lannes's corps and about 30,000 with Gudin's division, Höpfner); side A's losses (3,300 killed and wounded and 700 prisoners, Bodart; about 1,000 and then more, Lannes; 700 wounded and 400 killed, Corbineau; 6—700 dead and 1500 wounded as the French give them, about 7000 or by the official reports 10,000 as the Russians claim, Höpfner; the 3rd division's own line); side B's losses and guns (3,500 and 12 cannon, Bodart; 3500 by the Russian reports, over 2000 dead, 1500 wounded and 12 guns by the French, and no guns lost in the battle itself, Höpfner; over 3,000 left on the field and about 600 prisoners, Lannes; 2,000 wounded and stragglers in the town and 600 prisoners, Corbineau; 14 pieces abandoned near Moszyn on the march and 23 pieces to be abandoned, the journal, Davout and Daultanne); the Russian wings (on the town and the Mosino wood, Höpfner; on two bridges, Lannes); and the dragoon journal's 'Le 22', printed so for the day of the battle.

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his 66 Russian battalions and his 24 French battalions match Höpfner's, his 700 prisoners and Russian 3,500 match the figures in Höpfner, and his 12 cannon the French claim there, while his 75 squadrons, 200 guns, 44,000 and French 3,300 match no figure in the passages read); Foucart, Campagne de Pologne, t. I and t. II, one family with his Campagne de Prusse (the same author's edition of the French side's documents: the major general's letters of 25 and 26 December, Lannes's reports of 27 and 28 December, Corbineau's letter of 28 December with its hearsay, the extract of the 3rd corps's journal of operations, Davout's corps's own record, Daultanne's pencil note and report, Davout's letter, the editor's narrative and notes, a quotation of the 5th dragoon division's journal and the summary return); Höpfner, Bd. 3 (the Prussian side's history of the campaign, the same work and family as his first, second and fourth volumes; he gives Bennigsen's motives, dispositions and strength without naming a source, sets the Russian and the French reports against each other, gives the losses as each side gives them and judges the battle a Russian victory).
